name: Sundance yellow (1979)
description: Hughes Airwest's 'Sundance' scheme as worn in 1979: the whole aircraft a bright golden yellow, body, fin, rudder, the 727's center engine fairing and the nacelles alike, with a black radome and light frames round the cockpit windows. 'HUGHES AIRWEST' in the airline's own blue lettering (heavy, extended, forward-leaning capitals tied by long horizontal strokes) under the forward cabin windows, from the first window behind the door to about the wing. On the fin a large blue mark: three tall upright-sided parallelograms side by side whose tops and bottoms slope down toward the nose, so it reads as an M over a W. Gray wings and tailplane, the nacelles' inlet lips polished. Worn by the DC-9s and the 727-200s until the merger into Republic in October 1980.

logos.description: Hughes Airwest's mark in blue: three tall parallelograms side by side, their sides upright and their tops and bottoms sloping down toward the nose, so the top edge is a row of three sawteeth and the bottom another (an M over a W), with thin gaps of the fin's yellow between them. Painted facing forward on both sides.

titles.style: Hughes Airwest's own lettering in blue: heavy, extended, forward-leaning block capitals with square counters, the letters packed close and tied by long horizontal strokes (the S's and the T's bars run out under and over their neighbours, the A is a forward-pointing wedge). Under the forward cabin windows, from the first window behind the door aft.

notes: Measured 2026-11-24 for Skyarium's ghost flights. Hughes Airwest flew DC-9-10s and -30s and, from 1979, 727-200s; there's no DC-9 shape yet, so the scheme is drawn on the MD-82 (MD82), whose nose, forward door and cross-section are the DC-9-30's. The title is placed in meters from the forward door as on DC-9-31 N912RW (1976, side-on): from 1.84 m behind the door's middle, 8.87 m long, the capitals 0.60 m tall with their tops just under the centerline, about 0.35 m under the windows' middle. On the longer MD-82 it ends well ahead of the wing where on a DC-9-30 it reaches the wing root. The lettering leans forward the same way on both sides (N912RW's right side, N9332's left), as ordinary italics. The fin mark's size and place are shares of the fin's own outline on N912RW (its foot just above the root, about half the fin's height from the root to the top of the tailplane's fairing, its middle a little behind the middle of the chord). The body's paint has no edges to measure: everything but the radome, the window frames, the wings and the tailplane is yellow. In 1979-80 some DC-9s (N9337, N9332) had a bare metal fin with the mark on a yellow six-sided panel and bare nacelles; that variant isn't drawn. Radomes were mostly black in 1979 (N915RW, N9337, April 1979); some were yellow (N9339 in 1978, N9332 in 1980). The registration was lettered small in blue on the nacelle (N912RW, N915RW) or on the body just ahead of it (N9337, N9332) and isn't drawn; the blue lines round the doors aren't either. The 1979 photos show no US flag; N9332 had a small one over its forward windows by June 1980. The yellows on the slides range from lemon to deep gold with the film; the palette's is a middle reading of sunlit paint, not Hughes Airwest's specification. The scheme came in with the Hughes Air West name in 1971 (approximate here) and was worn until the merger into Republic (RC1979) on 1 October 1980.

B722.note: The 727-200's title starts about 1.1 m behind the forward door and runs about 19 window pitches, its capitals a little taller than the DC-9's, under the windows; the fin mark sits on the 727's short fin above the center engine's fairing, made to fill most of its height. Read off N721RW (January 1980), taken from below in flight, so both are approximate. The S-duct fairing, nacelles and body are yellow as on the DC-9s.
